raw_case_text:
A 21-year-old Mexican patient presented to Donghai Hospital with complaints of fever (39.3 C), anorexia, and watery diarrhea three to four times a day. About 16 days prior to the onset of these symptoms, he arrived in Yantai, China. His condition improved after 2 days of antipyretic and antidiarrheal treatment (clindamycin 900 mg, etimicin 100 mg, anisodamine 10 mg, dexamethasone 5 mg, and antondine 2 ml). Unfortunately, the patient developed abdominal pain (paroxysmal colic) and diarrhea on the third day after discharge, and the symptoms gradually worsened. Two days later, the patient went to Yeda Hospital. On admission, he appeared ill and jaundiced but was alert. Initial vital signs were temperature 37 C, blood pressure 120/65 mmHg, heart rate 100 beats/min, and respiratory rate 18/min. Abdominal physical examination revealed right upper quadrant tenderness without rebound tenderness, liver percussive pain, Murphy's sign, no kidney percussive pain, and no rash. Initial investigation (Table 1) showed acute infectious, hyperbilirubinemia, elevated transaminases, and thrombocytopenia. The hepatitis panel was negative. Rapid tests for Vibrio cholerae O1/O139 were also negative. Chest computerized tomography (CT) showed bilateral inferior lobar foci, right pleural hypertrophy, and adhesion. Abdominal CT indicated hepatosplenomegaly and cholecystitis. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) showed gallbladder enlargement and wall thickening, cholecystitis not excluded, bilateral pleural effusion, and a small amount of ascites. Blood culture revealed the growth of Gram-negative rod. After admission, he received a combined therapy of levofloxacin and imipenem. Due to his serious condition, he was transferred emergently to Yuhuangding Hospital at 9 pm the next day after admission.
On arrival at Yuhuangding Hospital, his vital signs were temperature 35.8 C, blood pressure 114/59 mmHg, heart rate 89 beats/min, and respiratory rate 20/min. Blood tests (Table 1) were notable for elevated transaminases, prolonged prothrombin time (15.2 s, activity 53.9%), high international normalized ratio (1.32), elevated D-Dimer, elevated serum amyloid A and procalcitonin, thrombocytopenia, and eosinopenia. Chest CT showed bilateral pneumonia and bilateral pleural effusion. Abdominal CT showed fatty liver, hepatosplenomegaly, thickening of the horizontal duodenal wall, multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the mesentery, cholecystitis, and a small amount of ascites (Figure 1). The following test results were negative: the full panel for hepatitis; serologic tests for hantavirus, EB virus, and TORCH (Toxoplasma gondii, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, and other pathogenic microorganisms); nucleic acid assay for cytomegalovirus, EB virus, and the new Bunya virus; fecal bacterial isolation of V. cholerae O1/O139 and Escherichia coli O157:H7. The patient received intravenous meropenem 1.0 g per 8 h. On the second night after the transfer, the patient had bloody stools with clots three times within 3 h, about 50, 100, and 300 ml, respectively. Three urgent blood tests showed a continuous decrease in hemoglobin and platelet count from 126 g/L and 42 x 109/L to 101 g/L and 26 x 109/L, respectively. Blood pressure dropped to 96/45 mmHg. He was rendered norepinephrine (400 mug/h), somatostatin (250 mug/h), vitamin K1 (20 mg, ivgtt), and hemocoagulase agkistrodon (2 IU, iv). The patient had another bloody stool about 200 ml 8 h after the first bloody stool. The electrocardiograph (ECG) monitor showed blood pressure 115/54 mmHg, heart rate 107 beats/min, blood oxygen saturation 99%, and respiration 24 beats/min. Urgent blood test showed hemoglobin 83 g/L, platelet count 43 x 109/L, prothrombin time 17.0 s, activity 46.0%, and fibrinogen 1.68 g/L. The patient received human prothrombin complex 600 IU and two infusions of O-type RH-positive RBCs (2.0 units and 1.5 units, respectively) without any transfusion side effects. On the third morning in Yuhuangding Hospital, Yeda Hospital reported the result of blood culture initiated at the time of admission, which was identified as S. Typhi. Transcatheter arterial embolization (TAE) refused by the patient initially was performed after 3 days of conservative treatment failed. Hemostasis was achieved and the patient continued to receive total parenteral nutrition and symptomatic support treatment (Figure 2). Unexpectedly, the patient had three more bloody stools (about 350 ml in total) with no obvious cause on the fourth day after TAE. Urgent blood test showed hemoglobin 66 g/L, neutrophil count 1.55 x 109/L, K 3.22 mmol/L, Na 134.7 mmol/L, Ca 1.86 mmol/L, Mg 0.64 mmol/L, glucose 8.07 mmol/L, creatinine 48 mumol/L, urea 1.47 mmol/L, uric acid 157 mumol/L, prothrombin time 13.1 s, D-Dimer 12.6 mg/L, and procalcitonin 0.466 ng/ml. The patient was then transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) and underwent TAE again. On the second day in the ICU, he had bloody diarrhea again. The hemoglobin level increased from 66 to 97 g/L after 4.0 units of RBC transfusion. On the third day in the ICU, the patient developed severe leukopenia (1.78 x 109/L) and was treated with recombinant human granulocyte stimulating factor (GSF; 100 mug subcutaneous injection) promptly. After 5 days of intensive care in the ICU, his vital signs stabilized. The patient was discharged after another week of comprehensive treatment in the general ward. He returned to Mexico immediately after discharge and did not receive follow-up examinations as prescribed.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 21-year-old Mexican male presented with fever of 39.3 °C, anorexia, and watery diarrhea, followed by severe paroxysmal colicky abdominal pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Fever (39.3 °C), anorexia, and watery diarrhea (3-4 times daily) started 16 days after arriving in Yantai, China. He received 2 days of outpatient antipyretic/antidiarrheal therapy with temporary relief, but developed severe paroxysmal colicky abdominal pain and recurrent diarrhea 3 days post-discharge, which progressively worsened over 2 days. He presented to a secondary hospital and was transferred to a tertiary center. On hospital night 2, he developed massive lower gastrointestinal bleeding (bloody stools with clots totaling ~450 mL over 3 hours, and another 200 mL 8 hours later) with hemorrhagic shock. Four days after initial embolization, he experienced recurrent lower GI bleeding (350 mL), followed by recurrent bloody diarrhea in the ICU.
subjective.past_medical_history: Recent international travel: arrived in Yantai, China from Mexico 16 days prior to symptom onset. Prior therapy for current illness: clindamycin 900 mg, etimicin 100 mg, anisodamine 10 mg, dexamethasone 5 mg, antondine 2 mL for 2 days.
subjective.review_of_systems: Anorexia, colicky abdominal pain, watery and subsequent massive bloody stools with clots. No allergies documented.

objective.physical_examination: Ill-appearing, jaundiced, alert. Vitals: temperature 37 °C initially (35.8 °C on transfer); blood pressure 120/65 mmHg initially, dropping to 96/45 mmHg during bleed, and 115/54 mmHg post-resuscitation; heart rate 100 beats/min initially, 89 beats/min on transfer, and 107 beats/min during bleed; respiratory rate 18-24/min; SpO2 99%. Abdomen: right upper quadrant tenderness without rebound tenderness, liver percussive pain, positive Murphy's sign, no kidney percussive pain; no rash.
objective.routine_investigations: Hematology: thrombocytopenia (platelets 42 x 10^9/L falling to 26 x 10^9/L) and eosinopenia; hemoglobin decreased from 126 g/L to 101 g/L, then 83 g/L, nadir 66 g/L (increased to 97 g/L after transfusion); neutrophil count 1.55 x 10^9/L; severe leukopenia in ICU (WBC 1.78 x 10^9/L). Coagulation: prolonged PT 15.2 s (activity 53.9%) to 17.0 s (activity 46.0%), INR 1.32, fibrinogen 1.68 g/L, elevated D-Dimer (12.6 mg/L). Inflammatory markers: elevated serum amyloid A, elevated procalcitonin (0.466 ng/mL). LFTs & Biochemistry: hyperbilirubinemia, elevated transaminases; K 3.22 mmol/L, Na 134.7 mmol/L, Ca 1.86 mmol/L, Mg 0.64 mmol/L, glucose 8.07 mmol/L, creatinine 48 umol/L, urea 1.47 mmol/L, uric acid 157 umol/L. Infectious workup: rapid tests and fecal isolation for Vibrio cholerae O1/O139 and E. coli O157:H7 negative; full hepatitis viral panel negative; serologies for hantavirus, EBV, and TORCH negative; PCR for CMV, EBV, and new Bunya virus negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT: bilateral inferior lobar foci, right pleural hypertrophy and adhesion, progressing to bilateral pneumonia and bilateral pleural effusion. Abdominal CT: fatty liver, hepatosplenomegaly, thickening of horizontal duodenal wall, multiple enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes, cholecystitis, and small amount of ascites. MRCP: gallbladder enlargement and wall thickening, cholecystitis not excluded, bilateral pleural effusion, and small ascites. Interventional angiography: emergency transcatheter arterial embolization (TAE) performed twice for active/recurrent intestinal bleeding.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Typhoid fever (Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi bacteremia) complicated by massive lower gastrointestinal hemorrhage, hemorrhagic shock, acute acalculous cholecystitis, bilateral pneumonia, and secondary myelosuppression (severe leukopenia). Confirmed by blood culture yielding Gram-negative rods identified as Salmonella Typhi. Antimicrobial therapy: initially IV levofloxacin and imipenem, switched to IV meropenem 1.0 g every 8 hours. Resuscitation for hemorrhagic shock: norepinephrine (400 mcg/h), somatostatin (250 mcg/h), IV vitamin K1 (20 mg), hemocoagulase agkistrodon (2 IU), human prothrombin complex (600 IU), multiple packed red blood cell transfusions (total 7.5 units), and total parenteral nutrition. Hemostasis achieved via two separate transcatheter arterial embolizations (TAE). Recombinant human G-CSF (100 mcg SQ) administered for severe leukopenia. Stabilized after 5 days in the ICU and 1 week in the general ward; discharged clinically recovered.
